news.title: These tech outages are giving Y2K, AI agent style
news.summary_raw: Are the recent outages in the airline booking systems, banking platforms, and productivity platforms really a coincidence? There's actually likely something deeper going on, cybersecurity experts say.
news.source_text:
It’s going down, as the American rapper Yung Joc might say: the airline booking systems, banking platforms, and productivity platforms. In the past two weeks, the U.S.’s top businesses have faced technical outages that have disrupted the systems that run everyday life.
Apple Pay went down. NASA’s internal communication network went down. The FAA had to ground all flights for hours (only the third time in history since 9/11), and Microsoft was hit with an outage that took down Outlook, Teams, and Copilot for nearly two days.
The first thought, naturally, is an AI hacker invasion of some sort, especially after hackers managed to attack fridges in a grocery store and a blood bank in France a few weeks ago. Here in the U.S., the director of National Intelligence said these outages don’t seem related to state-sponsored terrorism, while President Trump called the issues “individual events.” Many of the companies themselves have said the outages were not caused by cyberattacks or AI attacks, but tech issues.
Only, there’s the fact that they all struck within a short timespan of each other, and just a few weeks after Cybersecurity’s so-called “Black October,” when a slew of also-unrelated cybersecurity incidents occurred on October 21, striking PHP, Node.js, LiteLLM, more.
While there’s no reason to view these outages as cyberattacks, there may be more than coincidence going on: It’s giving AI-native Y2K, frankly.
Dave DeWalt, an investor who worked in cybersecurity for more than three decades (including as president and CEO of McAfee and as vice chairman of the CISA Advisory Council for the Department of Homeland Security), also thinks it’s probably AI-related.
The technical outages are most likely the “growing pains of a security system that’s getting stronger, not weaker,” and that “AI is surfacing vulnerabilities at a speed and scale we’ve never had before through AI tools like Mythos and others,” he told TechCrunch.
The thing is, many of these technical flaws have always existed, but because AI is surfacing them so fast, enterprises are rushing to fix them before bad actors can exploit them. “That surge in patching is disrupting things in the short term,” he said.
This was, perhaps, the first moment when legacy meets modern, Anusha Iyer, a software engineer and founder of the security startup Corsha, told TechCrunch. “These industrial systems were never designed to be connected, let alone securely connected in the way we are pushing them to be today,” she said.
Virginia Senator Mark Warner, vice chair of the Senate Intel Committee, came to a similar conclusion (although investigations are still underway as to what could be happening). “These disruptions should serve as a wake-up call. It feels like every day brings another reminder that AI is moving faster than our ability to manage its consequences,” the senator wrote on X.
AI is reshaping how software is built, deployed, and operated, on a scale where everyone feels the sharp learning curve. Iyer
news.summary: A spate of technical outages at major U.S. firms—including Microsoft, Apple Pay, and the FAA—has spurred speculation that AI‑driven vulnerability discovery is accelerating failure rates. Experts warn that AI tools are surfacing hidden flaws so rapidly that patching cycles are destabilizing critical services.
news.enterprise_use: Go to your Microsoft 365 admin center this week and verify that all automatic patching settings for Outlook, Teams, and Copilot are enabled, and that any delayed‑update policies are reviewed. Failure to do so risks prolonged downtime and could expose your organization to exploitation of newly discovered AI‑identified weaknesses. Microsoft 365 is the most affected platform here, so prioritizing its update compliance is critical.

news.title: Man hired by Russia spied on Silicon Valley tech and defense company, feds say
news.summary_raw: 25-year-old accused of stalking employees at coffee shop and in an "aggressive" car pursuit.
news.source_text:
A Russian national has been indicted on suspicions he was a Russian spy who stalked and surveilled employees of a Silicon Valley company that was assisting Ukraine in its ongoing war with its eastern neighbor.
Igor D’iu, 25, allegedly photographed the employees and their computer screens as they worked at a coffee shop located near the company’s Palo Alto office, federal prosecutors said Wednesday. He also kept a list of home addresses of employees and a senior executive. At one point, prosecutors said, D’iu trailed an employee as she traveled home from Palo Alto to San Francisco. An affidavit filed in the case referred to the employee as FEMP1, short for female employee, and said the event left her “in a state of emotional distress.”
Evasive and irregular turns
“FEMP1 made evasive and irregular turns, took back roads, and turned into a grocery store parking lot where D’IU continued aggressively following her vehicle,” an FBI special agent wrote. “D’IU followed FEMP1 through U-turns, illegal left turns, and ran a red light to stay with FEMP1 for nearly thirty miles. FEMP1 called 911 while driving and was instructed to drive directly to San Francisco Police Department (“SFPD”) Mission Station. Near SFPD Mission Station, FEMP1 flagged an SFPD patrol vehicle and reported the incident. D’IU left once FEMP1 made contact with the patrol vehicle.”
When police later questioned D’iu about the incident, the defendant allegedly said he saw a woman get into a car and thought she was “beautiful.” He then told the investigators that he followed her because he “wanted to ask her out on a date.”
Prosecutors didn’t name the company, but both Reuters and Bloomberg, citing unnamed people with knowledge of the case, identified it as Palantir. Ars is unable to confirm that reporting. Palantir representatives didn’t respond to an email seeking confirmation.
news.summary: A Russian national was indicted for spying on employees of a Silicon Valley tech company, allegedly photographing workers and tracking them in public spaces. The investigation highlights ongoing threats to employee privacy and corporate security for firms involved in sensitive defense projects.
news.enterprise_use: 1. Review and reinforce your employee security awareness program to cover physical surveillance risks. 2. Ensure all personnel are trained to recognize and report suspicious behavior and to use secure communication channels when discussing sensitive work. 3. Verify that your endpoint security and identity management tools (Google Workspace, JumpCloud, Freshservice) are configured to alert on anomalous login patterns that could correlate with physical security incidents.

news.title: A game you cannot win unless you have a quantum computer
news.source_text:
November 19, 2026
Shashwat Kumar and Rodrigo Cortiñas, Research Scientists, Google Quantum AI, Google Research
On a superconducting processor, we turned one of quantum mechanics’ strangest features into something you can measure, benchmark, and put to work across systems as large as 105 qubits.
Here is a Sunday paper-style puzzle you can try right now. Draw a 3×3 grid. Fill every cell with either +1 or −1, subject to two rules: each row must multiply to +1, and each column must multiply to −1.
Go ahead. We’ll wait…
You didn’t manage it, right? There is an elegant reason for that. For a row to multiply to +1, it needs an even number of −1s. For a column to multiply to −1, it needs an odd number. Add up the rows and you learn the grid contains an even number of −1s. Add up the columns and you learn it contains an odd number. Well…That’s impossible!
The grid would have to be two contradictory things at once. No such table exists; it is a paradox.
Now turn the puzzle into a game: Each round, Alice is handed a row and Bob a column. Without talking, Alice fills her row by the row rule and Bob fills his column by the column rule. They win if they put the same number in the square where their row and column intersect. Any plan made in advance is just a pre-written table, meaning at best they will win 8 out of 9 rounds. This changes if they use a quantum computer. It won't fill in the impossible grid, but in principle, it lets them win every round.
The reason is a property called quantum contextuality, arguably the strangest feature of quantum mechanics. Einstein once famously asked whether the moon is there when nobody looks, his way of insisting that physical properties ought to exist whether or not anyone measures them. For quantum systems, contextuality is the precise, experimentally testable statement that the answer can be no: you cannot assign fixed, pre-existing values to everything you might measure.
What a measurement yields can depend on which other compatible measurements you make alongside it (i.e., on its context). This is not only a deep philosophical statement, but more so, cutting-edge science and the basis of a new technology. And in the game above, Alice and Bob can use it to engineer a solution. Their answers are not looked up in a hidden table written in advance; the table does not exist. Their answers come into being as they measure, and quantum correlations stitch them together more tightly than any classical rulebook permits.
Entanglement usually gets top billing as the “magic ingredient” of quantum computing. But a growing body of theory suggests contextuality is the deeper resource, the thing that actually powers certain quantum algorithms past their classical counterparts. The catch is that, until recently, contextuality had been demonstrated almost exclusively in small systems of a few particles. Whether it survives, and stays useful, in the many-body systems that real quantum computers are made of was an open question.
That is
news.summary: Google Quantum AI researchers demonstrated that quantum contextuality enables a game to be won every round, a property that could underlie future quantum algorithms. The breakthrough showcases quantum mechanics’ unique feature beyond entanglement, potentially shaping advanced computing paradigms.
news.enterprise_use: No immediate action is required for your current IT stack. Keep the finding in mind for future strategic planning when quantum technologies become commercially available.

news.title: The unfolding Jensen Huang scandal: a timeline
news.summary_raw: Jensen Huang has resigned from Nvidia following an affair, which could have ramifications for national security as the U.S. and China race to develop the most advanced AI infrastructure.
news.source_text:
Nvidia co-founder and now former CEO Jensen Huang has never been as prone to controversy as AI leaders like OpenAI’s Sam Altman or SpaceXAI’s Elon Musk. But the 63-year-old industry kingpin recently admitted that he cheated on his wife of 40 years in affairs that could have ramifications beyond Huang’s personal life and U.S. national security.
U.S. officials believe that one of Huang’s likely romantic interests, Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, is a Chinese spy who has been feeding information back to Beijing. (Alice Huang, a Chinese citizen, is of no relation to Jensen Huang.)
Megaspeed is a Singapore-based AI infrastructure company that reportedly purchased $4.8 billion worth of Nvidia chips over the last two years. The U.S. and Singapore have both previously investigated Megaspeed over suspicions that the firm was illegally sharing chips with China. The Justice Department has since taken over the federal investigation into the company, The New York Times has reported.
The story took a sudden turn on Wednesday. Citing five people who worked at Nvidia, the Times reported that Huang also had an extramarital relationship with Kimberly Powell, the company’s vice president of healthcare, who reports directly to him. Nvidia, Huang and Powell have not confirmed the report. Reached by a Times reporter, Huang reportedly said, “I don’t think you should be talking to me directly,” before hanging up.
By early Thursday morning, Huang was no longer CEO of the company he co-founded 33 years ago. Then, Thursday afternoon, Reuters dropped another bombshell, publishing a report alleging that Huang had yet another extramarital affair with another unnamed Nvidia employee.
The U.S. and China are embroiled in a fierce technological arms race to build the most advanced AI infrastructure, which could shape each country’s economic future, military prowess, and capacity for innovation. Nvidia is valuable in this competition as one of the world’s largest makers of AI chips, which are essential for accelerating AI development. But as an American company, Nvidia faces government restrictions on the sale of its most powerful chips to Chinese entities.
As the controversy unfolds, we are organizing the most relevant events into a reverse-chronological timeline to keep you up to date.
November 17, 2026: Nvidia posts strong quarterly earnings, says it does not plan to reinstate Huang
Nvidia reported its quarterly earnings on Tuesday, which beat Wall Street expectations with $115.8 billion in revenue, up 103% year-over-year. Despite the unknowns the company faces without Huang involved, interim CEO Colette Kress said that full-year revenue is also on track to exceed expectations. The company also plans to raise its outlook for the 2028 fiscal year, indicating confidence that this unexpected leadership change won’t get in the way of its trajectory.
“We have the best technologists on the planet with a world-class multi-year roadmap,” Kress said. “From a business perspective, it’s
news.summary: Nvidia’s former CEO Jensen Huang’s personal scandal has escalated into a national security concern, with allegations that a Singapore-based AI company linked to him may be funneling Nvidia chips to China. The fallout has prompted a federal investigation and forced Nvidia to replace its CEO amid concerns over the company’s role in the U.S.-China AI arms race.
news.enterprise_use: Check your organization’s vendor risk assessments for any reliance on Nvidia GPUs or related supply chains; update compliance documentation to reflect increased scrutiny of Chinese partners.

news.title: Meta’s new Muse Charm device may cost $300
news.summary_raw: Meta hasn't denied the reporting from The Information, saying only that it will "have more to share soon" about its upcoming AI wearable.
news.source_text:
Meta plans to charge $300 for Muse Charm, its upcoming Tamagotchi-like AI device that was teased at the company’s Connect event earlier this year, The Information has reported.
When reached for comment by TechCrunch, a Meta spokesperson didn’t deny the claims, merely providing the following statement: “We’re charmed by the interest in our AI devices, and we’ll have more to share soon.”
So far, Meta has made a relatively successful push into consumer AI, launching Muse — its agentic helper — along with a variety of cute avatars that users can use to give the system more of a personality.
Muse Charm, the company’s push into AI hardware, will allow users to carry a physical personification of its software around in their pocket (or potentially wear it around their neck), talking to it, asking it questions, and giving it commands.
It remains to be seen whether customers will bite or not. AI wearables have had a rough go of it so far (here’s looking at you, Humane Ai pin), but companies continue to iterate on the concept in an attempt to break through to a broader audience.
Indeed, $300 is arguably a pretty steep price for a product the size of a keychain, although it’s also a price point that’s in line with what other companies have been charging. The wearable launched by Friend — the AI startup whose device lets you text and talk to an AI persona — is currently retailing for $250. On the other hand, Amazon’s all-new Bee Frontier wearable AI device — which transcribes conversations and tracks tasks — lists for $75 and is currently on a Black Friday, 30% off sale of $52.49. Even with its $99/year subscription to let it tie into a user’s apps (photos, emails, etc.), it’s still far less expensive than Muse Charm.
news.summary: Meta plans to launch Muse Charm, a $300 AI-powered wearable that lets users carry a physical avatar of its Muse assistant. The device, announced after teasing at Connect, aims to blend consumer AI with tangible interaction, but faces a high price point and uncertain market demand.

news.title: Pancreatic cancer halted by virus injection in three patients
news.source_text:
A virus has stopped pancreatic cancer in its tracks in three people in a clinical trial in the US. Further evaluation is needed in larger trials, but the early results are encouraging, especially since only small doses of the virus were administered for initial safety testing.
“We only injected one-tenth of the dose we are eventually aiming at, so the efficacy is better than I expected, especially as this is pancreatic cancer,” says Masato Yamamoto at the University of Minnesota, who led the development of the viral treatment.
Pancreatic cancer is notorious for being the deadliest type of the condition. One reason is that symptoms tend to appear late, when the cancer has already spread and cannot be surgically removed. Once diagnosed, people usually live only around three to six months.
Advertisement
Another reason is that pancreatic tumours have tough, fibrous exteriors that block chemotherapy drugs from getting in. “They’re hard as hockey pucks,” says Yamamoto. Immunotherapies that boost immune activity against cancer are also ineffective, because pancreatic tumours can hide from the immune system.
The first patient in the trial, who had a pancreatic tumour 7 centimetres across, was administered the treatment a year ago, and the other two have been since then. At the time, their tumours hadn’t spread beyond the pancreas. Since being treated, their tumours haven’t grown any further. “They are all still alive and have clinically stable disease,” says Yamamoto, who presented the results at the annual meeting of the American Society of Gene and Cell Therapy in Boston, Massachusetts, earlier this month. Another 15 patients will now be given higher doses to find the optimum level.
“I think this is an interesting early signal, but as a pancreatic surgeon, I think it’s important to keep perspective,” says Kai Brown at Royal North Shore Hospital in Sydney. “The history of oncology is littered with promising early signals that vanished by the time rigorous phase III [late-stage] testing was done, so I think these preliminary conference results should probably just be seen as hypothesis-generating at this stage.” He also notes that the trial so far hasn’t included a control group, so it is hard to know whether the cancer-killing virus works better than other treatments or none at all.
The virus is an adenovirus that has been genetically engineered to replicate only inside tumours and not healthy tissue. Its replication is specifically activated by an enzyme called cyclooxygenase-2 (COX-2), which is present at much higher levels in cancer cells than in normal ones. After cancer cells become infected with the virus, they burst open and die, releasing more virus that can infect neighbouring cancer cells.
In the trial, the virus was injected directly into the patients’ tumours through a thin tube that was guided down a patient’s throat to their pancreas. The tube had an ultrasound probe on the end to allow visualisation of the tumours.

news.summary: A genetically engineered adenovirus halted tumor growth in three pancreatic cancer patients during a clinical trial, with early results presented at a recent conference. The therapy uses a COX‑2‑activated virus injected directly into tumors via a guided tube.
news.enterprise_use: This development has no immediate impact on your IT infrastructure or workflow. Keep it as background context for future discussions on healthcare data security or clinical trial data management.

news.title: Apple may be developing its own AI agent that runs your Mac
news.summary_raw: The iPhone maker appears to be building agents that can compete with the likes of Meta Muse, Instinct, Claude, and OpenAI Dots.
news.source_text:
Apple appears to be working on its own AI agent to conduct computer work on behalf of users — including using apps, accessing websites, and coding, among other things.
The news was originally reported by Bloomberg, which spotted a job listing the iPhone maker recently posted for a senior engineering manager to oversee the creation of an “AI agent that can use a computer.”
“Imagine an AI agent that can use a computer the way a capable person does,” the posting says. “It browses the web, works across apps, runs commands, writes and debugs code, and calls services, and it chooses the right tool for each step. It does all this privately and with the polish people expect from Apple.”
The posting additionally notes that the agents should be able to move “fluidly between tools” and “carry out multi-step tasks across apps, browsers, command lines, code, and APIs.”
TechCrunch reached out to Apple for more information but did not receive a response.
Agents capable of computer work have become one of the hottest commodities in the tech industry over the past year. Major labs like Anthropic and OpenAI have launched such services, while other major tech brands — like Meta, which recently launched its Muse agent line — have also moved into the space. It makes sense that Apple — which is trying to expand its AI offerings in the new John Ternus era — would want to follow suit.
Bloomberg additionally notes that, at the same time that Apple is working on its own digital assistant, the company is making it significantly harder for third-party agents to gain total control over its computers.
The outlet notes that the version of its upcoming macOS 27.3 will deploy warnings discouraging users from granting full access to third-party agents. In October, Apple issued a notification to developers stating that the company planned to “introduce additional controls to ensure that users who genuinely wish to grant an app this extraordinary level of access can only do so with very explicit user action.”
Bloomberg writes that while the iPhone maker “has eyed introducing the service as soon as the end of next year,” progress on its in-house agent “remains in the early stages.”
news.summary: Apple is reportedly developing an AI agent that can autonomously use macOS apps, browse the web, and execute code, signaling a shift toward integrated computer assistants on Mac devices. The company is also tightening controls to prevent third‑party agents from gaining full system access, a move that will affect macOS security policies and endpoint management.
news.enterprise_use: Go to your MDM and endpoint security dashboards this week to review the upcoming macOS 27.3 control changes—especially the new warning prompts for granting full agent access. Failing to update your policies could expose Macs to unverified AI agents that might bypass existing security layers, while early adoption of the controls will keep your environment compliant with Apple’s stricter access model.

news.title: Introducing harness adapters: adapt your favorite model to your harness to improve performance and cost
news.source_text:
Introducing harness adapters: adapt your favorite model to your harness to improve performance and cost
Combining RL on a custom task distribution with your favorite agent harness yields more accurate and efficient models for that target harness and task distribution.
Models are not fully optimized for all harnesses and the tasks you’re doing. Instead, they target general performance. So when you combine a model and harness, you’re leaving performance and efficiency on the table for the stuff you’re actually doing. With RL, you can train a custom harness adapter that squeezes everything out of your model for your harness and task combination.
Take Qwen3.8-27B, its Terminal-Bench 2.1 score with the pi harness is 39% which uses on average 2.9K tokens per task. If we freeze those weights and add a custom RL-trained LoRA adapter we can get 55% pass@1, with average token usage of 1.5K. Most of this is down to the model reasoning less, calling less tools, and performing better first time.
Our earlier work (multi-harness RL, harness adapters) showed that RL on your own task distribution, inside your own harness, gives a more accurate and more efficient model. Those experiments covered data-analysis and code-building tasks. Here we wanted to push this further by exploring whether the result holds at 27B, on harder real-world software engineering tasks, across three harnesses: Pi, OpenCode and Hermes Agent. And most of all, share a fully reusable recipe, so you can reproduce this on your own task, harness, model combinations.
TL;DR
- We trained one LoRA adapter for Qwen3.8-27B per agent harness (pi, Hermes Agent, OpenCode), with RL inside the harness itself.
- Datasets, training and agent rollouts all happen on the Hub in Jobs using TRL's AsyncGRPOTrainer, OpenEnv and harbor.
- Each harness adapter beats the base model under its own harness on both benchmarks, for both performance and efficiency.
- The three LoRAs are also merged into a single super adapter that runs unchanged under pi, Hermes Agent and OpenCode.
- All artifacts (adapters, GGUFs, RL tasks, safeagents plugin) can be browsed through this Hugging Face collection.
Table of Contents
- Training inside agent harnesses
- Generating custom RL tasks on Hugging Face
- Testing the filters with short training runs
- AsyncGRPOTrainerfor more efficient GRPO training
- Training setup
- Super-adapter: merging all adapters into one
- Final results
- Open question: What did the model really learn to do?
- Closing words and future directions
Training inside agent harnesses
We leverage the Harbor integration in OpenEnv and TRL’s OpenEnv guide to train the model inside the harnesses we chose for the final training. We have built ready-to-use docker images for all our RL tasks that come with the target harnesses already pre-installed inside. In our final docker images, we use Pi 1.5.2, OpenCode 2.2.7 and Hermes Agent v0.22.6. The diagram below from the aforementioned blogpost explains well the entire protocol:
news.summary: Hugging Face releases harness adapters that let users fine‑tune large language models with reinforcement learning inside specific agent harnesses, boosting performance and cutting token usage. The adapters are available as reusable LoRA models and can be deployed via the Hugging Face Hub and Docker images for Pi, OpenCode, and Hermes Agent harnesses.
news.enterprise_use: Review the Hugging Face adapter repository to determine if your internal AI tools (e.g., custom code‑analysis bots or data‑analysis pipelines) could benefit from a lightweight LoRA fine‑tuning that reduces token consumption. If you already use a Hugging Face model in any of your CI/CD or monitoring workflows, test the super‑adapter on a small sample task this week to benchmark efficiency gains.

news.title: Frostbite: A new CPU architecture discovered, designed and verified by AI
news.summary_raw:
Article URL: https://architectlabs.com/blog/frostbite
Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50572503
Points: 353
# Comments: 228
news.source_text:
Introducing Frostbite: A new CPU architecture discovered, designed, and verified end-to-end by AI
Abstract
In our previous post, Redwood, we showed that given an architecture, our AI systems could implement, verify, and deploy an inference accelerator in record time. However, similar to other scientific domains, we believe that AI systems, given the correct freedom and guardrails, can co-design software and hardware together, making optimizations across the stack and opening a design space so large it was previously inaccessible. We set out to answer the question: “Could our AI systems & tools lead to a novel hardware discovery that radically outperforms human-made designs?”
Today, we're introducing Frostbite, a general-purpose CPU with a new instruction set built from the ground up. Frostbite exploits the properties of interaction nets, namely that every step is local, every dependency is explicit, and every value has exactly one owner, to reach a step-function gain in CPU performance that has long stagnated. On a set of 25 initially chosen workloads, including 15 held out until the final evaluation, we achieved a 4.59x performance-per-watt multiple when compared to a modern, silicon-proven superscalar (dual-issue, in-order) CPU core.
Our AI systems autonomously iterated over the compiler, ISA, architecture, microarchitecture, RTL, verification, and final GDS. When we took a closer look at the discovered architectural primitives, we were surprised to find novel hardware implementations and runtime features that would have otherwise been difficult to architect. In spite of stagnation in CPU core improvement, we were able to take a workload concept all the way to a final GDS, and prove a step-function increase in perf/W and perf/area. We believe that as AI systems become more capable, every class of chip we know today, from datacenter-grade CPUs, to AI accelerators, to networking switches and NICs, will go through similar fundamental architectural shifts.
Introduction to interaction nets
Mainstream programming languages, when compiled for general-purpose CPUs, hide the dependencies between the parts of a program. Any piece of code may read or write any variable through a shared, mutable state, and so modern CPU hardware assumes the worst case and rediscovers, at runtime, which instructions actually depend on each other. Moreover, single-core CPU performance has largely stalled since the early 2000s, pushing people towards large multicore CPUs such as Intel Xeon, AMD Zen, and NVIDIA Vera. This forces CPUs to maintain the illusion that every core sees the same memory, and keeping that illusion consistent and performant requires deep cache hierarchies and coherence protocols that cost area and power, and scale poorly.
Interaction nets1 take a different approach. A program is a graph of nodes, and computation happens by rewriting pairs of nodes that are connected through their ports. Every rewrite only touches a small, local part of the graph. Because
news.summary: Redwood AI unveiled Frostbite, a fully AI-designed general‑purpose CPU that promises a 4.59x performance‑per‑watt boost over current silicon cores. The architecture leverages interaction nets to achieve unprecedented efficiency through local, dependency‑explicit computation.
news.enterprise_use: Review the Frostbite whitepaper and benchmark results to assess potential impact on future data‑center hardware procurement. Consider engaging with Redwood AI or similar research partners to explore whether AI‑co‑designed CPUs could reduce power or cooling costs for your cloud workloads. Keep an eye on any commercial availability timelines, as a shift in CPU design may affect vendor lock‑in and the relevance of existing hardware optimization scripts.

news.title: Muse Is Unleashing a World of Pettiness on Instagram
news.summary_raw: Meta’s AI assistant can track and unfollow Instagram users who don’t follow you back—and some people are taking full advantage.
news.source_text:
Khalil Roberts had heard horror stories of people getting kicked off Instagram for using third-party apps to purge follower counts, so when he came across an X post claiming that Muse—Meta’s AI assistant—could mass-unfollow people who didn’t follow him back, he didn’t believe it.
“I’ve never gone through my exact list to vet those people out, but I’ve always been curious,” the 31-year-old New Yorker tells WIRED. But after realizing that by using Muse, his account wouldn’t get flagged as spam, his mind was made up. “I was like, I actually will be a little petty.”
After downloading Muse, Roberts, who had over 7,600 followers, entered the prompt: “Can you show me a list of people (non celebrity) that [don’t] follow me back on instagram and can you unfollow them for me. ”
Within minutes, Muse identified 151 accounts. It attached an Excel sheet with a breakdown of everyone cataloged—separated by categories identifying their username, real name, classification, and profile link—and asked if Roberts wanted to proceed with his request. Shockingly, some of the names were people he thought of as friends. “It was a little surprising, but also a reminder that we don’t have a relationship anymore.”
Following the success of his November 7 cleanse, Roberts posted about it on X, offering instructions to his followers. Over the past several weeks, parallel scenarios have played out across X, Instagram, and Facebook, with users sharing tips on how to automate their unfollows with the help of Muse.
X user @justdrmj posted about the trend the same week as Roberts, and nearly every reply shared a taste for trivial grudge-holding. For him it came down to one simple rule: “Why be a fan?” “i agree. reciprocity is key,” one person said in response. “The way I just cleaned house,” added another. In a seeming outburst of celebration, one X user posted: “Just unfollowed 1000+ people on IG.”
Even tech worker Kimberly Munoz, who has 33,200 Instagram followers, said she wasn’t about to be “anybody’s fan,” noting in an Instagram video that she used the feature to suss out “people that I know in real life that have unfollowed me.” “I downloaded Muse just to do this only,” one person responded.
With social media rapidly evolving, there is no longer a unified consensus around etiquette. For some people, following others is an indication of friendship or simply a way to keep tabs on your latest crush. Others view it as more of a social obligation—you follow someone if they follow you, but the opposite is true as well.
Natalie Pennington, an associate professor who researches social connection at Colorado State University, wonders about the consequences of people gradually outsourcing small social decisions to technology.

news.summary: Meta’s AI assistant Muse now enables users to mass‑unfollow non‑reciprocal Instagram accounts with a single prompt, streamlining social media clean‑ups. The feature has sparked widespread use on Instagram, X, and Facebook, raising questions about automated social decisions.

news.title: This 16-Year-Old Founded an AI Missile Startup. He’s Targeting ‘Cost per Kill’
news.summary_raw: Henrijs Dandzbergs dropped out of high school to join startup accelerator Y Combinator. With a new breed of missile, he wants to make killing as efficient as possible for the US and its military allies.
news.source_text:
At 16 years old, Henrijs Dandzbergs is too young to vote. Or drink. Or smoke. Or drive unsupervised. But he’s not too young to win half a million dollars for his AI-guided-missile startup.
In September, Dandzbergs, who was born in Latvia, was admitted to Y Combinator’s fall 2026 cohort. The startup accelerator counts companies like Airbnb, Stripe, DoorDash, and Reddit among its alumni; Dandzbergs is likely the youngest solo founder in its vaunted history.
His startup, Polemos Industries, is attempting to develop a new class of precision-guided missile that can be easily and cheaply manufactured, can be fired from portable launchers, and can resist jamming attempts. “I think missiles are the coolest thing,” Dandzbergs tells WIRED. “A lot of people that have found success in engineering early on have had a passion for blowing stuff up.”
In conversation, Dandzbergs is poised and articulate. He talks about “attacking hard problems,” breaking things down to “first principles,” and how the Ukraine conflict has forever altered the theater of war—a personal fixation, given his country's proximity to Russia. He projects an unassailable confidence in his own abilities.
“He’s a pretty exceptional person,” says Harj Taggar, a YC partner assigned to mentor Dandzbergs. “I’m still somewhat in disbelief that we’re talking about a 16-year-old.”
Dandzbergs has resolved to apply these unusual talents to figuring out how to optimize targeted killing. His startup’s guiding ambition, according to its investor one-pager, is to bring down the “cost per kill.”
As a young(er) kid, Dandzbergs was rarely in one place for long; his family moved between Latvia, Indonesia, Australia, and Spain. His surfer father, part owner of an insurance company, likes to go wherever he might find the raddest waves.
Early in his schooling, which mostly took place online, Dandzbergs demonstrated a clear talent for science and math. His room started to look like a lab, littered with schematics, robotics, Raspberry Pis, and 3D-printed components.
When Covid struck, Dandzbergs’ family returned to Latvia. His parents enrolled him in Astra Nova, an Elon Musk–linked school where students undergo an experimental curriculum built around lateral thinking and problem-solving instead of rote memorization. Dandzbergs took a class taught by a NASA employee and became fascinated by aerospace engineering. His lab creations became ever more elaborate: a bionic arm, a thermal control system for a model rocket, sensors for a self-flying drone.
Around this time, Russia invaded Ukraine. In Latvia, Dandzbergs started to see military jets overhead, and stray missiles were intercepted at the Russian border. With the sovereignty of Eastern European nations under threat, new defense startups began to pop up across the region. Dandzbergs wanted in.
“A patriotic intention to protect my country, European countries, and Ukrainian and American soldiers, and understanding the future of autonomous warfare—that’s my drive,”
news.summary: A 16‑year‑old founder, Henrijs Dandzbergs, has launched Polemos Industries, a Y Combinator‑backed startup aiming to create low‑cost, AI‑guided missiles that can be manufactured cheaply and resist jamming. The venture focuses on precision‑guided weaponry, targeting a reduction in the "cost per kill" through autonomous targeting.

news.title: If you can't explain something in simple terms, you don't understand it (2017)
news.summary_raw:
Article URL: https://kottke.org/17/06/if-you-cant-explain-something-in-simple-terms-you-dont-understand-it
Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50572355
Points: 270
# Comments: 162
news.source_text:
If you can’t explain something in simple terms, you don’t understand it
In the early 1960s, Richard Feynman gave a series of undergraduate lectures that were collected into a book called the Feynman Lectures on Physics. Absent from the book was a lecture Feynman gave on planetary motion, but a later finding of the notes enabled David Goodstein, a colleague of Feynman’s, to write a book about it: Feynman’s Lost Lecture. From an excerpt of the book published in a 1996 issue of Caltech’s Engineering & Science magazine:
Feynman was a truly great teacher. He prided himself on being able to devise ways to explain even the most profound ideas to beginning students. Once, I said to him, “Dick, explain to me, so that I can understand it, why spin one-half particles obey Fermi-Dirac statistics.” Sizing up his audience perfectly, Feynman said, “I’ll prepare a freshman lecture on it.” But he came back a few days later to say, “I couldn’t do it. I couldn’t reduce it to the freshman level. That means we don’t really understand it.”
John Gruber writes the simple explanations are the goal at Apple as well:
Engineers are expected to be able to explain a complex technology or product in simple, easily-understood terms not because the executive needs it explained simply to understand it, but as proof that the engineer understands it completely.
Feynman was well known for simple explanations of scientific concepts that result a in deeper understanding of the subject matter: e.g. see Feynman explaining how fire is stored sunshine, rubber bands, how trains go around curves, and magnets. Critically, he’s also not shy about admitting when he doesn’t understand something…or, alternately, when scientists as a group don’t understand something. There’s the spin anecdote above and of his explanation of magnets, he says:
I really can’t do a good job, any job, of explaining magnetic force in terms of something else you’re more familiar with, because I don’t understand it in terms of anything else you’re more familiar with.
Feynman was also quoted as saying:
I think I can safely say that nobody understands quantum mechanics.
Pretty interesting thing to hear from a guy who won a Nobel Prize for explaining quantum mechanics better than anyone ever had before. Even when he died in 1988 at the end of a long and fruitful careeer, a note at the top of his blackboard read:
What I cannot create, I do not understand.
news.summary: This article reflects on Richard Feynman's teaching philosophy, emphasizing the importance of being able to explain complex concepts simply as proof of understanding.
